about:
> *Half Life is the unfortunate condition of all things.*
>
> Nothing maintains its proper shape for very long. Cities rearrange themselves. Familiar places disappear. Friends scatter toward distant shores. Great enthusiasms become mild curiosities, and occasionally the reverse. Even you, despite whatever assurances you may have made on the subject, are becoming someone else.
>
> This is generally considered alarming.
>
> I have elected to find it interesting.
>
> Half Life is my attempt to keep some record of the transformation: photographs, journeys, projects, people, objects, observations, and whatever peculiar business happens to occupy my attention before it inevitably gives way to something else.
>
> I make no promise that these records will be complete, useful, or even entirely sensible. Completeness is an exhausting ambition, and usefulness has already been addressed elsewhere on this site.
>
> The important thing is that one remains conscious. Still looking. Still wanting. Still wandering about with unreasonable plans.
>
> Everything is already changing.
>
> One may as well go see what it becomes.

posts.title: Entry 6
posts.body:
*An account of ten days spent upon the island of Oʻahu, where nature proved magnificent, the provisions abundant, and the affairs of men predictably troublesome.*

Our days upon the island unfolded with considerably less regard for my carefully constructed itinerary than I had originally intended. This was not, I hasten to explain, the result of poor planning. Rather, Hawaii possesses an extraordinary abundance of distractions, and I have never considered it wise to remain enslaved to a schedule when fortune presents a more interesting proposition.

Thus our adventures proceeded according to a system of calculated improvisation, a method in which I possess considerable expertise.

We climbed the ancient volcanic heights of Diamond Head, where the morning sun illuminated Waikīkī beneath us. The ascent was agreeable, particularly with the assistance of my mechanical Hypershell, a contrivance acquired during my earlier travels through China. Martina accompanied me, and together we admired the coast while I attended to the important business of photography.

Koko Head proved a considerably more formidable adversary. Its thousand and more railway ties ascended the mountainside with such merciless determination that I began to suspect their architect had harbored a profound resentment toward mankind. Yet with the assistance of my mechanical apparatus and the application of my considerable resolve, I attained the summit. The view was magnificent, though I maintain that the mountain might have furnished an equally satisfactory spectacle with half the required suffering.

Our wanderings carried us across the windward coast, where the Mokulua islets rose from the turquoise waters beyond Lanikai. We climbed the Pillbox ridge in the early light, visited the tranquil Byodo-In Temple, and wandered among the astonishing green mountains of Kualoa. The great cliffs appeared almost impossibly arranged, as though some extravagant deity had sculpted them for the express purpose of impressing travelers.

At Makapuʻu we surveyed the vast Pacific, while at Halona we watched the sea force its way through the volcanic shore. We explored Kailua and its neighboring beaches, where the waters possessed colors which I would ordinarily accuse a painter of inventing.

The northern coast offered wonders of a different character.

At Laniākea Beach we encountered a magnificent Hawaiian green sea turtle, known locally as a *honu*, resting upon the sand with the indifference of an ancient sovereign. The creature appeared entirely unmoved by the admiration of its visitors, an attitude I found thoroughly respectable. Here was a being which commanded attention without making the slightest effort to solicit it. I have known men who spent their entire lives attempting to cultivate such dignity, only to be surpassed by a reptile whose principal ambition appeared to be remaining comfortably upon the beach.

We observed it respectfully from a distance, allowing the creature its peace. I departed with considerable admiration for its philosophy of indifference, though I confess that I have seldom found occasion to practice it myself.

In Waimea Valley we walked beneath dense tropical greenery toward the waterfall, and from the heights of the Ehukai Pillbox we surveyed the celebrated Banzai Pipeline, where enormous waves broke upon the shore with sufficient violence to discourage my participation.

I have never considered it necessary to risk drowning merely to demonstrate that I possess courage. My survival, after all, is of considerably greater value to the world.

We wandered through the banyan trees at Kawela Bay, where I photographed Martina beneath their extraordinary branches. Later, upon the sands of Sunset Beach, I made further portraits as the golden light faded and a nearly full moon rose above the coast.

These were among my favorite moments of the journey. Martina possesses a natural ease before the camera, and I found great pleasure in preserving her likeness amid such remarkable surroundings. The photographs will endure long after the warmth of those evenings has become a distant memory.

Our explorations also led us into the rainforests above Mānoa, where the earth appeared determined to conceal itself beneath an extravagant quantity of vegetation. We walked through bamboo forests toward Mānoa Falls, wandered the grounds of Lyon Arboretum, and followed damp trails through the green valleys above the city.

At Foster Botanical Garden we encountered ancient trees of immense proportions, while Hoʻomaluhia presented a tranquil lake beneath the towering Koʻolau mountains. The landscape was so extravagantly green that I briefly suspected some botanical enchantment had escaped the supervision of its creator.

At Pali Lookout, the wind attempted to remove us bodily from the mountain. Having already endured the hostility of the atmosphere during our arrival, I regarded this renewed aggression with contempt and refused to be intimidated.

Our adventures were not confined to mountains and forests.

We spent considerable time wandering through Chinatown, exploring galleries, curious shops, and bakeries filled with pastries of every description. We visited ʻIolani Palace, where the history of the Hawaiian monarchy offered a sobering account of sovereignty, ambition, and the consequences of power exercised without justice.

The palace was particularly memorable, for it reminded me that beneath the island's agreeable climate and magnificent scenery lies a history far more complicated than the entertainments offered to visiting travelers.

Naturally, our explorations required frequent nourishment.

At Leonard's we obtained malasadas so fresh that the sugar seemed scarcely prepared to accept its responsibilities. At Marukame we enjoyed steaming bowls of udon, while Morning Catch provided poke of such quality that we found ourselves returning for another meal.

We ate shrimp in Kahuku, an undertaking which produced considerable satisfaction and an equally considerable quantity of sauce upon our fingers. The shrimp were magnificent, though the meal required a degree of manual involvement which might have offended a more delicate constitution. Fortunately, I possess no such weakness.

We sampled poke and shave ice along the windward coast, and breakfasted at Kalapawai and Koko Head Cafe, where the provisions proved particularly welcome after our various mountain ascents.

Our evening meals were a subject of considerable interest, though not every celebrated establishment proved deserving of its reputation.

The Vietnamese cooking at The Pig and the Lady was excellent beyond reasonable dispute, while Senia likewise demonstrated considerable culinary talent.

Fête, however, was another matter entirely.

I had approached the establishment with expectations encouraged by its considerable reputation. What followed was a meal of perfectly respectable mediocrity. Nothing was especially offensive, yet nothing inspired admiration. The food was merely adequate, an unfortunate achievement for a kitchen which appeared to regard itself as something rather more distinguished.

I found the experience decidedly middling.

Curiously, its sister establishment, Heyday, situated within the White Sands Hotel, proved vastly more agreeable.

Here I discovered a burger of such satisfying character that I returned upon several evenings to renew our acquaintance. Some might regard repeated consumption of the same dish as evidence of limited imagination. I consider it the conduct of a man who has identified a reliable pleasure and sees no advantage in gambling upon an inferior alternative.

More remarkable still was the Bloody Mary.

I have consumed this particular concoction in numerous establishments, and my standards have become correspondingly severe. Yet the version served at Heyday was of such excellence that I placed it confidently among the ten finest I have encountered.

A considerable distinction, and one which I do not bestow lightly.

Thus I found myself in the peculiar position of preferring the supposedly lesser establishment to its more celebrated relation. An instructive reminder that reputation is merely the opinion of others, while good judgment is the privilege of those fortunate enough to possess it.

Then there was the matter of tonkatsu.

Martina had previously declared one preparation to be the finest of her life, an assessment I respected while declining to endorse with equal enthusiasm. Later, at Tamafuji, we encountered pork cutlets of such exceptional crispness that I was obliged to reconsider the standards by which such dishes ought to be judged.

I shall not claim that we reached a definitive agreement. A relationship between two intelligent persons must allow for occasional differences of opinion, particularly concerning matters as consequential as fried pork.

Yet not every undertaking proceeded according to our designs.

We had arranged an expedition to the Big Island, intending to inspect its volcanic wonders. Lodging had been secured, a carriage reserved, and dinner arranged at the Fish Hopper. Dee accompanied us, bringing the practical wisdom of a man who had previously endured the incompetence of commercial airlines.

Approximately ten minutes before boarding, our flight was canceled on account of a mechanical difficulty.

What followed was an hour of waiting, a telephone conversation with an agent whose speech advanced more slowly than continental drift, and a series of proposals which failed to satisfy even the most charitable interpretation of reasonable travel arrangements.

I demanded a manager, examined the alternatives, temporarily secured a later flight, and ultimately obtained full refunds for our party.

The volcano remained unseen.

I regarded this as a regrettable failure on the part of the airline, though the recovery of our money offered some consolation. A man may be deprived of an adventure, but he need not permit the responsible parties to profit from his disappointment.

With our afternoon unexpectedly liberated, Martina and I purchased inexpensive snorkeling equipment and entered the sea.

Beneath the surface we discovered an astonishing abundance of fish moving among colorful coral. The underwater world proved so lively that I began to suspect we had obtained the better portion of the day's entertainment after all.

We concluded the afternoon with photographs of the sunset, followed by food and drink at our hotel.

Thus the airline's incompetence had inadvertently provided us with an agreeable day beside the sea. I would not recommend its methods, but I could scarcely dispute the outcome.

Throughout the journey, our good friend Dee remained a most welcome companion. His generosity, humor, and familiarity with the island greatly enriched our travels. I have praised this gentleman before and see no reason to diminish my assessment now. It is a rare privilege to find a friend whose company remains agreeable across such a variety of circumstances, from excellent meals to bureaucratic disasters.

Martina also found opportunities for her own discoveries, including a visit to Aaila, where she selected a perfume after careful consideration. I admired her discernment, though I confess that my own attention was frequently divided between the fragrances, the surrounding shops, and the possibility of our next meal.

As our journey approached its conclusion, I devoted further attention to photography. At Magic Island we watched the sunset illuminate the coast, while Kaimana Beach offered a final morning view of Diamond Head.

We also visited Photobox in Ala Moana, where Martina and I obtained portraits together. Having spent much of the journey photographing landscapes and my companion, I found it fitting that we should preserve at least one record in which we both appeared.

At last, the hour of departure arrived.

We returned our elderly but dependable Turo carriage to South Drive and proceeded to the airport, where an airship awaited to carry us back to San Francisco.

I considered the journey as a whole.

We had climbed mountains, wandered through ancient forests, explored unfamiliar neighborhoods, encountered creatures of land and sea, and eaten with an enthusiasm which I consider entirely appropriate to a successful expedition.

We had laughed with a trusted friend, discovered remarkable places, and accumulated photographs which would preserve a portion of our experiences against the inevitable erosion of memory.

Not everything had proceeded as intended. Certain destinations escaped us, arrangements were altered, and one particularly ambitious expedition ended before it began.

Yet I have come to suspect that a journey's worth cannot be measured solely by the number of objectives completed.

The world is too large, its diversions too numerous, and its inhabitants too unpredictable for even the most carefully constructed itinerary to survive entirely intact.

A clever traveler must therefore possess not only the foresight to make plans, but the judgment to abandon them when circumstances offer something better.

In this respect, I consider our Hawaiian expedition an unqualified success.

posts.title: The Hypershell Entry 1
posts.body:
Among the innumerable contrivances devised by the ingenuity of mankind, there are few which command my interest so readily as those intended to improve upon the limitations of the human body. I have long regarded our natural construction as a respectable but unfinished achievement. The arms are serviceable, the eyes reasonably competent, and the legs, though useful under ordinary circumstances, possess the regrettable habit of surrendering their enthusiasm precisely when the journey becomes interesting.

It was therefore with considerable satisfaction that, during my travels through China some months ago, I acquired a device known as the Hypershell.

This remarkable apparatus, a mechanical arrangement secured about the hips and thighs, has been designed to assist the wearer in the ancient and frequently tiresome business of walking. By means of mechanisms whose inner workings I shall leave to men of narrower but more specialized genius, the device reduces the effort demanded of the legs, thereby allowing its operator to travel greater distances with less expenditure of his own vitality.

A most sensible invention.

For centuries mankind has labored to produce machines capable of carrying him across continents, oceans, and the heavens, yet until comparatively recently has devoted insufficient attention to the indignity of having to propel himself across the ground once he arrives. The Hypershell represents a welcome correction to this oversight.

I first put the device to use during our extensive wanderings through China, where the distances demanded of the traveler frequently exceeded the reasonable expectations of his anatomy. There it performed admirably, assisting me through long days of exploration and confirming my suspicion that mechanical ingenuity, properly employed, may compensate for certain shortcomings in nature's original design.

Upon returning home, however, the device saw regrettably little service.

The preceding year had found me frequently upon the trails, pursuing mountain summits, forest paths, and other destinations which sensible men might reasonably observe from a comfortable distance. This year, by contrast, has been devoted more extensively to travel. My adventures have carried me across oceans and into foreign lands, leaving fewer opportunities for the familiar pleasure of setting out into the wilderness near home.

I do not regret the exchange. A man cannot reasonably complain of insufficient adventure merely because his adventures have become geographically extravagant.

Nevertheless, I missed the mountains.

Our recent expedition to Hawaii therefore presented an excellent opportunity to renew my acquaintance with the Hypershell and subject it to a series of practical trials.

The first occurred upon Diamond Head.

Now, I must make clear that Diamond Head is not, by any reasonable measure, a particularly formidable ascent. Its paths are well established, its summit readily attainable, and its principal difficulty lies in the determination of its visitors to arrive at the same hour. A man of ordinary constitution may complete the climb without recourse to extraordinary equipment, provided he has not spent the preceding evening indulging too enthusiastically in food and drink.

Yet I saw no reason to refuse the assistance of a machine merely because the task was within my natural abilities.

A clever man does not insist upon suffering when he has already purchased the means of avoiding it.

With the Hypershell secured about my person, I ascended the mountain with remarkable ease. The device performed its duties so effectively that the climb seemed scarcely more demanding than an agreeable morning stroll. I reached the summit with sufficient energy remaining to admire the view, operate my photographic apparatus, and contemplate the curious spectacle of other travelers laboring upward through their own unaided efforts.

I regarded them without contempt. After all, not everyone has yet discovered the advantages of mechanical enlightenment.

The true examination, however, awaited me at Koko Head.

Here the mountain presented a considerably less charitable arrangement.

More than a thousand railway ties ascend the volcanic slope in a long and merciless procession, each one seemingly positioned to extract a further measure of effort from the unfortunate climber. The incline grows increasingly severe, and the summit remains visible throughout much of the ordeal, a circumstance which I consider a particularly cruel feature of its design.

There is something deeply offensive about being permitted to see one's destination while being required to suffer so extensively in reaching it.

I began the ascent with the Hypershell secured firmly in place.

The machine assisted me faithfully, though I shall not insult the reader's intelligence by claiming that the climb became effortless. The mountain remained steep, the steps remained numerous, and my lungs continued to demand their customary tribute.

Yet I possessed a confidence which I might otherwise have found difficult to maintain.

I knew that I would reach the summit.

The Hypershell did not abolish the difficulty of the undertaking, but it rendered the difficulty manageable. There is an important distinction between a machine which removes all exertion and one which enables its operator to continue despite it. The former would be a luxury; the latter is an instrument of considerable practical value.

And so I climbed.

Step followed step, the slope grew more severe, and the mountain continued its stubborn refusal to become any shorter. Yet my mechanical companion persisted in its assistance, and at length I emerged upon the summit, victorious over the railway ties and their architect's apparent hostility toward mankind.

The view was magnificent.

Below me stretched the coastline, the volcanic crater, and the broad Pacific, whose waters seemed entirely indifferent to the exertions required to behold them from such a height.

I stood there with considerable satisfaction, though I was not so foolish as to mistake the machine's assistance for an absence of personal achievement. The apparatus had contributed its mechanical strength, certainly, but it was I who had directed the enterprise, endured the ascent, and selected the destination.

A general does not surrender credit for a victory merely because his soldiers possess excellent weapons.

Several days have since passed, allowing me to consider the experience with greater detachment.

I have concluded that Koko Head, though unquestionably difficult, was not the most punishing ascent of my recent travels.

That distinction belongs to the thousand steps I climbed in Zhangjiajie, during our earlier expedition through China.

The comparison is an interesting one.

Both climbs demanded considerable effort. Both rewarded their visitors with views of exceptional beauty. Both appeared to have been devised by persons who regarded stairs as a suitable substitute for human kindness.

Yet Zhangjiajie exacted a greater price.

I recall reaching the heights of those extraordinary Chinese mountains and finding myself breathless for a period considerably longer than I would have preferred. The landscape was magnificent, with immense pillars of stone rising through the mist like the ruins of some forgotten celestial kingdom. Yet the grandeur of the scene did little to persuade my lungs that their obligations had been fulfilled.

Koko Head was a severe undertaking, but Zhangjiajie had tested me more thoroughly.

I record this distinction not as a criticism of either mountain, but as a matter of historical accuracy. A man who has conquered several formidable ascents must maintain a proper accounting of their respective difficulties, lest posterity be deprived of the information necessary to appreciate his achievements.

As for the Hypershell, my admiration for the device has only increased.

It is not a miraculous instrument. It cannot transform a mountain into level ground, nor can it entirely relieve the body of its natural responsibilities. Yet it provides a measurable advantage, and I have always held that an advantage, however modest, becomes formidable when placed in the hands of a sufficiently resourceful individual.

Indeed, I find myself increasingly interested in the future of such things.

The next object of my curiosity is a new generation of spectacles being developed by Google, those ingenious devices which promise to place information directly before the wearer's eyes.

I await their arrival with particular interest.

Some years ago, the same company attempted a similar undertaking, producing spectacles of considerable ambition but uncertain social acceptance. The invention was remarkable in conception, yet the world appeared insufficiently prepared to receive it. Whether the fault lay with the device, its creators, or the public's limited imagination remains a question worthy of debate.

Now the company proposes to return to the enterprise.

I am curious to discover what lessons have been learned.

Have the engineers corrected the shortcomings of their earlier design? Have the intervening years produced improvements sufficiently substantial to justify renewed enthusiasm? Or shall we witness another expensive demonstration of mankind's ability to invent a marvelous object without first determining whether anyone wishes to wear it?

These questions occupy me with considerable interest.

For we have arrived, by all appearances, in that future which earlier generations described with such extravagant confidence. Machines now converse with their operators, assist their movements, and promise to extend the reach of human perception. Devices once confined to speculative fiction have begun appearing in shops, advertised with the casual assurance ordinarily reserved for household appliances.

I find the development enormously pleasing.

There is, of course, a certain absurdity in the spectacle of a man fastening machinery to his legs in order to climb a mountain which he has voluntarily chosen to ascend. Yet I consider this no more absurd than constructing an airship to cross an ocean, or a camera to preserve an instant which would otherwise disappear forever.

Civilization advances through the refusal of ingenious persons to accept inconvenience as an unavoidable condition of existence.

And I, possessing a healthy appreciation for ingenuity, intend to enjoy the benefits.

Let other men insist upon accomplishing every task through the unaided exertions of their natural faculties. Let them climb their mountains with aching legs, consult their maps with downcast eyes, and regard every mechanical improvement as an affront to some imaginary purity of human endeavor.

I shall take a different course.

posts.title: Entry 5
posts.body:
There are few places in this world where the very air seems pleased by one's arrival. Hawaii, I have discovered, is among them.

We descended from the heavens and emerged from the airship into a warmth of such agreeable character that I immediately suspected the island had made certain preparations in anticipation of our coming. The breeze was neither the cruel, bone searching wind of northern cities nor the suffocating breath of some miserable desert. Rather, it moved across the skin with a peculiar gentleness, as though the atmosphere itself had been instructed to receive us with courtesy.

I have traveled sufficiently to know that the winds of the world are, as a rule, ill-mannered creatures. Yet here was a breeze which asked nothing, demanded nothing, and appeared content merely to welcome the traveler. A rare disposition, and one I found worthy of immediate approval.

Awaiting us at the port was Dee, that remarkable gentleman whose virtues I have previously catalogued at some length, and whose continued excellence threatens to exhaust my supply of favorable adjectives.

He had come bearing leis, fragrant garlands of flowers which he placed upon us in accordance with the customs of the island. I accepted this distinction with the grace befitting a man accustomed to ceremonial honors, though I understood that the gesture was one of friendship rather than recognition of my considerable achievements. Martina, whose delight in such occasions is both genuine and infectious, received hers with evident pleasure. The flowers suited her splendidly, though I suspect the island's entire botanical kingdom would have struggled to produce an arrangement capable of improving upon her natural charm.

Thus adorned, we departed in Dee's carriage toward our lodging.

Our first undertaking was a matter of baggage. We had arrived before the appointed hour at which our chambers were to be surrendered into our possession, a curious arrangement by which an establishment may accept one's coin long before it is prepared to accept one's person. Nevertheless, the attendants offered to safeguard our belongings and convey them to our room once it became available.

I regarded this promise with cautious optimism. Hospitality is a noble profession, but I have learned that promises made across a counter are not always fulfilled with the enthusiasm in which they are delivered.

With our burdens temporarily relinquished, Dee conveyed us to the location of our hired carriage, secured through an arrangement known as Turo.

The vehicle awaiting us was a venerable specimen, having evidently survived a considerable number of seasons and perhaps several changes in the prevailing civilization. Its finest years were undoubtedly behind it, though I saw no reason to hold this against the machine. I have known men of great age who remained useful long after their appearance suggested otherwise, and a carriage need not possess youthful splendor to fulfill its appointed function.

It had wheels, an engine, and every appearance of being capable of transporting us about the island without immediate catastrophe. These qualifications satisfied my requirements. I had not come to Hawaii to conduct an exhibition of mechanical elegance.

Our conveyance secured, we returned to the hotel to inquire after our chambers and exchange our traveling garments for attire more appropriate to the island's generous climate.

Here we encountered our first genuine astonishment.

The attendants had not merely kept their word concerning our baggage; they had conveyed it directly to our room, which was situated upon the third floor. I confess that this demonstration of competence exceeded my expectations. The prospect of dragging our possessions upward through three levels of architecture after a day of aerial confinement had been one I regarded with particular distaste.

Instead, our belongings awaited us in perfect order.

I was sufficiently impressed that I briefly considered offering the establishment a formal commendation, though I ultimately concluded that my continued patronage would serve as an adequate expression of gratitude.

Our chambers overlooked the pool, where other guests pursued their various aquatic amusements with an enthusiasm which suggested they had either recently discovered water or possessed an abundance of leisure. The view was agreeable, the room satisfactory, and the arrangement of our belongings entirely to our liking.

We exchanged our garments for lighter attire, and thus restored to a condition suitable for the tropics, set forth upon our first proper exploration of the island.

Our destination was the celebrated shore of Waikiki.

There we found a great expanse of sand bordered by waters of remarkable color, while the evening light settled upon the coast with the extravagance of a painter determined to exhaust his entire collection of pigments. The sea moved with a lazy confidence, sending its waves toward the shore as though performing some ancient ceremony whose meaning had long since been forgotten.

The beach was alive with humanity. Travelers wandered in various states of dress and undress, swimmers challenged the surf, and innumerable persons stood gazing toward the horizon with expressions of profound contemplation. What revelations they expected to obtain from so much water I cannot say, though I myself found the spectacle sufficiently impressive without requiring it to disclose any cosmic secrets.

Martina and I walked along the shore in Dee's company, taking in the sights and the agreeable disorder of the place. I found particular satisfaction in having at last reached this distant corner of the world with two people whose company I value so highly.

There are journeys which become tedious through the inadequacies of one's companions. This, I was pleased to observe, would not be among them.

We walked for a considerable distance, and although the scenery remained pleasing, our bodies eventually presented a united petition concerning the absence of nourishment.

Hunger is a most democratic affliction. It makes no distinction between the philosopher and the fool, the nobleman and the beggar, or a man of extraordinary faculties and his perfectly respectable associates. All must eventually submit to its demands.

Our first intended establishment appeared to be one of those fashionable dining houses whose tables must be secured through arrangements made well in advance, perhaps before one has even conceived the journey. I regarded this custom as a particularly tiresome expression of modern civilization. That a man should be expected to predict his appetite several weeks into the future strikes me as an unreasonable demand upon his powers of foresight.

We therefore passed it by.

Fortune, which occasionally displays an admirable willingness to cooperate with my designs, directed us instead toward an establishment specializing in tonkatsu.

Here we were presented with portions of breaded pork, fried to a pleasing golden finish and accompanied by the customary provisions. The meal was excellent, and I consumed it with the appreciation due to a kitchen which had plainly mastered its chosen craft.

Martina, however, was moved to a considerably higher degree of enthusiasm.

She declared the tonkatsu to be the finest she had ever tasted.

This was a pronouncement of no small consequence, for she possesses a discerning palate and is not ordinarily inclined to bestow such honors without justification. I listened to her assessment with interest, sampled my own portion once more, and considered whether some subtle perfection had escaped my notice.

After due reflection, I arrived at a different conclusion.

The tonkatsu was good.

Indeed, it was very good. Excellent, certainly. I could discover no substantial fault in its preparation, texture, or flavor. Yet I could not, in good conscience, proclaim it the supreme achievement of all pork cookery.

I explained this distinction with the delicacy appropriate to a man who values domestic harmony. Martina remained entirely convinced of her judgment, and I, recognizing that further debate would produce neither enlightenment nor additional portions, permitted the matter to rest.

Thus we enjoyed an excellent meal, though history must record that our respective assessments differed by a degree of enthusiasm.

By this hour, the accumulated burdens of travel had begun to make themselves known. The long passage through the heavens, the acquisition of our carriage, the arrangements at our lodging, and our extended promenade along the shore had together exhausted a respectable portion of our vitality.

Even I, whose reserves of determination are considerable, recognized the wisdom of concluding the day's proceedings before fatigue reduced us to creatures of mere instinct.

We therefore resolved to part company.

Dee, maintaining the same generosity with which he had received us, conveyed us once more to the hotel. We exchanged farewells and established our intention to meet again upon the following day, when the island would have further opportunity to reveal its curiosities.

I was grateful for his companionship and assistance. A man may possess all the cunning in the world, yet there remains considerable advantage in having a trusted friend awaiting him upon foreign shores.

Martina, having endured the day's exertions with admirable good humor, soon surrendered herself to sleep.

I, however, remained awake.

Beyond our chambers came the distant sounds of the hotel and its inhabitants. Laughter rose from the pool below, mingling with indistinct conversations and the occasional splash of water. Somewhere beyond the buildings, the sea continued its endless business with the shore.

I lay listening, my thoughts wandering among the events of the day and the possibilities of those yet to come.

We had arrived safely. Our accommodations were secured. Our carriage, though elderly, stood ready for service. We had walked the famous shores of Waikiki, eaten well, and renewed our friendship with a man of uncommon worth.

Beside me slept the woman I love, while beyond our window an unfamiliar island continued its nocturnal revelries.

For once, there was no urgent scheme requiring my attention, no adversary demanding correction, and no calamity from which I was obliged to extricate myself through some brilliant exercise of ingenuity.

I found the absence of these inconveniences surprisingly agreeable.

Still, as the laughter drifted upward from the pool and sleep continued to elude me, I could not help but contemplate the days ahead. An entire island lay before us, filled with strange landscapes, hidden pleasures, and opportunities whose nature I had yet to determine.

It seemed improbable that such a place could remain entirely undisturbed by my presence.

posts.title: Entry 4
posts.body:
# Arrival Upon the Island

My beloved and I have at last arrived upon the island, having entrusted ourselves to an airship of considerable dimensions, questionable engineering, and accommodations evidently devised by a man harboring some ancient grievance against the human spine.

The toll demanded for our passage was extravagant. For such a sum, one might reasonably expect a measure of comfort, perhaps even the occasional indulgence. Instead, we were assigned seats of such unyielding construction that I began to suspect the proprietor had mistaken the transportation of passengers for the punishment of criminals. Nevertheless, I bore these indignities with characteristic fortitude, reasoning that the discomforts of the journey would only serve to embellish the magnificence of our eventual arrival.

My companion, a woman of uncommon intelligence and excellent judgment, had elected to accompany me upon this expedition. This was a decision I regarded with considerable satisfaction, for although I am perfectly capable of navigating the world's treacheries alone, I have discovered that triumphs are considerably more agreeable when shared with someone whose company one genuinely enjoys.

Our passage through the heavens was, for a time, uneventful.

Then the winds, having apparently learned of my approach, resolved to make themselves disagreeable.

A tremendous gale struck the airship with such violence that the entire vessel shuddered upon its course. Its metallic bones groaned, the overhead compartments rattled, and the passengers surrendered themselves to a most undignified display of alarm. Women shrieked, children wailed, and several gentlemen of imposing appearance abruptly abandoned whatever claims they might previously have entertained concerning their own courage.

I alone, or so it seemed to me, maintained a proper appreciation of the circumstances.

It was evident that the atmosphere had taken some personal objection to our passage. I considered this an act of considerable presumption. Having already surrendered a substantial quantity of coin to the airship's proprietors, I was in no disposition to permit a collection of unruly vapors to interfere with my itinerary.

Indeed, I had made certain calculations concerning the matter. The winds, however powerful, possessed no discernible intelligence. I, conversely, possessed intelligence in abundance, together with an inflexible determination to reach the island. The outcome of such a contest could hardly be regarded as uncertain.

Thus I remained seated, regarding the commotion with the composure of a man who had already settled the question of his survival.

My beloved was beside me, and I found additional satisfaction in knowing that whatever absurdities the heavens might devise, we would face them together. She is no timid creature requiring constant reassurance, and I would insult her considerably were I to suggest otherwise. Indeed, I suspect that had the winds presented themselves in human form, she might have offered them a few observations sufficiently pointed to send them retreating toward the horizon.

In due course, the gale exhausted its objections, and the airship continued onward. Whether this retreat resulted from the pilot's efforts, some favorable atmospheric development, or the winds' belated recognition of their adversary, I shall leave to the judgment of posterity.

We descended upon the island at an hour which might reasonably have been assigned either to an afternoon meal or the conclusion of a respectable day's labor. The peculiar displacement of time had thoroughly disordered my reckoning. I briefly considered consulting a clock, but reflected that an instrument incapable of agreeing with my own internal chronology was hardly deserving of confidence.

Upon our arrival, we were greeted by none other than the remarkable gentleman of whom I have spoken so favorably in an earlier account.

I shall refrain from repeating the full inventory of his virtues, lest the reader accuse me of excessive generosity. Such accusations would be particularly offensive, as I am not ordinarily inclined to distribute praise without first establishing that the recipient has earned it.

This gentleman, however, remains a rare exception.

His faculties are formidable, his character unusually sound, and his capacity to influence the designs of other men is such that, were he possessed of a more ambitious temperament, I suspect several governments would presently find themselves operating under his direction without quite understanding how the arrangement had come about.

Yet he prefers a modest existence, displaying that curious restraint which so often accompanies men of genuine ability. I admire this quality enormously, though I confess that, were I endowed with such influence, I might be tempted to employ it toward rather more spectacular ends.

He received us warmly, and presently we departed in his carriage.

Now, it should be understood that I had already secured a carriage of my own for the duration of our stay. I am not a man who arrives upon foreign shores without having made certain provisions for his convenience. Nevertheless, it occurred to us that dispatching two carriages toward the same destination would constitute an extravagance of the most pointless variety.

Furthermore, as guests, we considered it entirely appropriate to accept our friend's hospitality. My own conveyance could remain at our lodging until some future occasion demanded its services.

Thus, through the application of sound judgment and a welcome economy of effort, the matter was resolved to everyone's satisfaction.

There is little else to recount concerning this first day.

No tyrant was overthrown, no fabulous treasure discovered, and no elaborate deception required the exercise of my more exceptional talents. The island, perhaps wisely, offered no immediate resistance to our presence.

Instead, we enjoyed the company of a trusted friend, exchanged stories, and surrendered ourselves to laughter of the most agreeable kind.

I found particular pleasure in seeing my beloved welcomed so warmly. She and our host were already acquainted, and their easy familiarity spared us the tedious ceremony of introductions. There is a peculiar happiness in seeing those whom one holds in high regard enjoy one another's company, particularly when one may take some modest credit for having assembled so distinguished a gathering.

And so our first day concluded without calamity.

We had crossed a great expanse of sky, endured the indignities of commercial aviation, defied the hostility of the winds, and arrived safely upon a distant island. We had been received by a friend whose company I value immensely, and I had beside me the woman whose presence makes even the most uncertain journey worth undertaking.

A lesser man might dismiss such a day as uneventful. I, possessing a more refined understanding of fortune, recognize that not every victory requires the humiliation of an enemy or the acquisition of wealth.

Sometimes it is sufficient to arrive precisely where one intended, in the company of precisely those with whom one wishes to be.

posts.title: Entry 3
posts.body:
My departure draws near, and a formidable multitude of preparations remains to be undertaken. Naturally, I have accomplished nothing.

First, provisions must be secured for The Cat, whose continued existence during my absence is a matter of considerable importance, particularly to himself. Fortunately, I have enlisted the services of a nearby devotee of felines, a person of trustworthy disposition and, I am assured, sufficient affection to prevent the creature from perishing through neglect. Thus, one obligation may be considered settled, though the provisions themselves remain conspicuously absent.

My bottomless bag, an indispensable article whose present condition renders its title a cruel mockery, has yet to be repaired. I must deliver it to a craftsman before my departure, lest I be forced to carry my possessions in the barbarous fashion of ordinary travelers.

Then there is the matter of film. My photographic ambitions are considerable, and I should regard it as a personal affront to posterity were some magnificent spectacle to present itself while my camera stood empty.

Most troubling of all, I have not packed a single article. My house, too, remains in a condition that demands attention, for I should prefer to return to a civilized dwelling rather than the aftermath of some minor catastrophe.

Thus I find myself besieged by obligations, each perfectly reasonable in isolation, yet collectively forming a conspiracy against my leisure.

Still, I possess two advantages: a quantity of time, rapidly diminishing, and an inexhaustible capacity for indecision.

Of these, the latter has proven by far the more dependable.

posts.title: Entry 2
posts.body:
With so many matters presently in motion, I have decided that further contemplation of the past would constitute an irresponsible misuse of the present. The old accounts may wait. There are expeditions to organize.

In the days soon to come, I intend to assemble a small but exceptionally capable company of men and sail for Treasure Island. Our purpose is singular and, I believe, culturally significant: to capture the finest photograph yet made of the San Francisco skyline. Should we succeed, the resulting image shall be displayed here at some considerably later date, once sufficient time has passed for the public to receive it properly.

For this undertaking I shall require two or three men of various builds, temperaments, and useful dispositions.

First, a land surveyor: one intimately familiar with the city, its peculiar geography, its winds, elevations, secret prospects, and the many locations from which San Francisco most enjoys being admired.

Second, a pack hauler: of sturdy constitution and cheerful obedience, who shall relieve me of those instruments necessary to my art but whose weight I find personally objectionable.

Finally, a charming fellow: of easy speech and flexible principle, whose purpose shall be to secure our passage through ports, gates, checkpoints, and whatever minor authorities presume to stand between us and destiny.

I shall, naturally, assume the role of mystic: consulting the heavens, interpreting the light, inspecting cloud formations with grave concern, and periodically pointing toward the horizon as though privy to information unavailable to ordinary men.

If all perform their duties admirably, glory is probable.

My second voyage shall be grander still.

By airship I shall depart for a distant island, a place reputed to restore both body and soul and return a weary traveler to civilization with an improved complexion and considerably better opinions about life.

I have visited this island before and can personally attest that the legends are true. Indeed, my spirit remains somewhat irresponsibly ignited from my previous pilgrimage. I therefore return in pursuit of those mysteries that escaped me the first time: warm waters, magnificent meals, long and idle afternoons, and that gentle breeze drifting in from parts unknown, carrying upon it the sweet scent of youth.

For an expedition of this importance, one cannot travel with ordinary company.

I shall therefore be accompanied by a woman of singular distinction, my girlfriend.

Her qualifications are numerous and difficult to summarize without embarrassing lesser persons. She possesses excellent taste, formidable curiosity, an instinctive understanding of beauty, and the rare ability to enter a place and immediately improve its general condition. Where I tend toward maps, equipment, unnecessary schemes, and solemn declarations of purpose, she possesses the considerably rarer faculty of knowing what is actually worth doing.

She is neither porter, assistant, nor decorative passenger. She travels under her own authority.

She too seeks the legends.

Indeed, I suspect the island may surrender certain secrets to her which it has deliberately concealed from me. This possibility is irritating, but I have made peace with it.

Fortunately, we shall not wander blindly.

Awaiting us is a guide most trusted, a man whom I consider a close brother and whom my companion already knows well.

It is difficult to describe this man without appearing to exaggerate, and so I shall make no attempt to restrain myself.

He is possessed of such uncommon ability that, were ambition his principal defect, entire institutions might presently operate according to his whims. He could, I suspect, bend the wills of sensible men toward almost any design and have them thanking him afterward for the privilege.

Yet he has chosen peace.

He lives humbly. He crests one mountain only to discover another behind it. He counts the grains of sand and, rather than declaring himself master of the coast, concludes that he has yet to understand the beach.

Such men are inconveniently rare.

His studies are now drawing to a close, and soon he will seek some grander stage upon which to deploy his talents. What form that stage shall take, I cannot say. I only know that the world will shortly have to contend with him.

Before that hour arrives, however, I intend to meet him upon this island one final time.

Thus the voyage carries purposes beyond leisure. I go to restore the spirit, pursue certain legendary gifts, rediscover an enchanted place beside a woman of extraordinary consequence, and share a few more idle days with a brother before the currents of life carry us toward different shores.

There will also, I am told, be drinks with little umbrellas in them.

The island awaits.

posts.title: Entry 1
posts.body:
Hello,

For some considerable time I have entertained the notion that I ought to have a website. The reasons for this conviction remain somewhat obscure, but the conviction itself has proved remarkably durable. At last, through a combination of industry, vanity, and an unexpected abundance of free time, the thing now exists.

My present scheme is to begin with several long and shamelessly retrospective accounts of the year thus far: projects undertaken with varying degrees of competence, places visited, objects made, and other episodes which, through the generous distortions of memory, now seem worthy of documentation.

Whether any of this will prove useful to anyone is doubtful. Fortunately, usefulness was never among the requirements.

Once I have exhausted accounts of the recent past, I shall concern myself with the future.
